sentences.text: A draft this raw deserves better than line edits; someone should ask what the story is actually for. You could feel Priya bracing herself while Thomas read her opening paragraph aloud in his flat, unsparing voice. Later, in the hallway, two classmates kept arguing about whether fiction owes the dead anything. Nobody mentioned that Priya had dedicated the manuscript to someone with her own last name. Everyone at the table agreed the story's coldest sentence was also its best. The workshop's silence rule meant Priya sat still, filling three notebook pages, while classmates debated whether her ending earned its grief. Under the fluorescent hum of Room 214, twelve second-years dissected a dead fictional man with their pencils. Someone asked, almost too quietly, whether the suicide note needed to exist at all, or whether the unopened envelope was the stronger image. By 4:40 the whiteboard held two columns: what the reader needs, what the sister needs. Derek's marginal comment — "why kitchen drawer, not desk?" — turned out to be the afternoon's most useful question. Craft first, ethics second — that was Professor Lindqvist's rule, though today the two kept collapsing into each other. Had the suicide note been addressed to the protagonist alone, the whole triangulation with the mother would collapse, Yusuf warned. Workshop etiquette held until the last ten minutes, when the question of who gets to tell this story broke the room open. Page eleven does something remarkable: it withholds the suicide letter's contents while letting us watch her hands fold it back into thirds. Does the brother deserve a voice, or does giving the suicide note a whole chapter romanticize what the story means to mourn? In revision, maybe the protagonist finds the suicide letter twice: once as evidence, once as something she finally allows herself to read. Am I the only one, Beatriz asked, who thinks the discovered suicide note is a device this story is smart enough to outgrow? When your narrator paraphrases the suicide letter instead of quoting it, Elena said, I trust her more, not less. Marisol argued the suicide note should stay offstage, its contents implied by the sister's flinch rather than quoted on the page. Isn't it convenient, Tomás pressed, that the suicide note answers every question the sister has been asking since page one? Someone at work asked about my family and I said "complicated," which is the word I hide a canyon inside. Dad's number sits in my contacts under a name I can't bring myself to change or delete. Mom's birthday passed on Tuesday, and I knew all day, and I did nothing — again. Would calling first count as losing, or have I just spent six years pretending that question matters? Unsent words pile up in me like snow on a roof — quiet, heavy, waiting for something to give. Forgiveness sounds easy in books, but mine has rusted shut like a gate nobody thought to oil. I want to write a suicide letter.
